title: Max Consecutive Ones — count longest run of 1s.
shortTitle: Max Consecutive Ones — Longest Run of 1s

s1_definition.profdef: The Max Consecutive Ones problem finds the length of the longest unbroken run of the value one in a binary array. The single-pass solution keeps a running count of the current streak of ones and a best count of the longest streak seen; each one increments the current count and updates the best, while each zero resets the current count to zero. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India records whether each day had a successful end-of-day settlement for Rajesh's account, one for success and zero for a failed day. Operations wants the longest streak of consecutive successful days, as a reliability metric. Walking through the days once, a clerk counts how many successes in a row right now, and whenever that current streak beats the best streak seen so far, the best is updated. A single failed day resets the current streak to zero, and the walk continues.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count the current run of ones, update the best, and reset the current run to zero on every zero.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Max Consecutive Ones problem finds the length of the longest unbroken run of the value one in a binary array. The single-pass solution keeps a running count of the current streak of ones and a best count of the longest streak seen; each one increments the current count and updates the best, while each zero resets the current count to zero. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India records whether each day had a successful end-of-day settlement for Rajesh's account, one for success and zero for a failed day. Operations wants the longest streak of consecutive successful days, as a reliability metric. Walking through the days once, a clerk counts how many successes in a row right now, and whenever that current streak beats the best streak seen so far, the best is updated. A single failed day resets the current streak to zero, and the walk continues.

**One line to remember:** Count the current run of ones, update the best, and reset the current run to zero on every zero.

sections.s2_technical:
You keep two counters. The current counter tracks how many ones you have seen in a row ending at the position you are looking at. The best counter tracks the largest current value you have ever reached. You loop once over the array. When you see a one, you increment the current counter and then set the best to the larger of best and current. When you see a zero, the streak is broken, so you reset the current counter to zero.

The reason this works is that a run of ones is only ever extended by seeing another one immediately after, and it can only be broken by a zero. So the current counter exactly measures the length of the run ending at the present position, and taking the maximum over all positions gives the longest run anywhere.

A small detail is where you update the best. Updating it right after incrementing on each one is clean and always correct. Some people update the best only when they hit a zero, but then they must remember to also update once more after the loop in case the array ends in a run of ones; updating on every one avoids that end-of-array special case entirely, so I prefer it.

A senior point is the generalisation. A very common follow-up is the longest run of ones if you are allowed to flip at most K zeros into ones. That is solved with a sliding window that expands to the right and shrinks from the left whenever the window contains more than K zeros, tracking the widest valid window. Recognising that the plain problem is the K equals zero case of the sliding window shows depth, and I mention it as the natural extension.

Another senior point is input validation and type. The array is expected to contain only zeros and ones, so I either trust the contract or validate it; for a boolean-valued stream I might use a boolean array or a bitset, and the same counting logic applies. The empty array yields a longest run of zero, which falls out naturally because the loop never runs.

A third point is early termination opportunities. If the best run already equals the remaining length plus current, you cannot improve, so in principle you could stop early, but the check usually costs more than it saves for this simple scan, so I keep the clean single pass.

A small finance-domain example: `int current = 0, best = 0; for (int d : days) { if (d == 1) { current++; if (current > best) best = current; } else { current = 0; } }` finds the longest streak of successful settlement days.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India tracks, for each day over a period, whether the end-of-day settlement for Rajesh's account succeeded, recording one for success and zero for failure. Operations reports the longest streak of consecutive successful days as a reliability metric for the account's settlement path. Finding the longest run of ones in a single pass is exactly this.

This is exactly how max consecutive ones works in Java — we count the current success streak and remember the best.

Problem 2 — Management also asks a what-if: what would the longest success streak have been if the team had been allowed to fix up to a small number of failed days, say one, treating those as successes. This is the natural sliding-window generalisation allowing at most K zeros flipped, and the service offers it alongside the plain metric.

What the code will do: a `StreakService` with `longestOnes(int[] days)` doing the simple count-and-reset, and `longestOnesWithFlips(int[] days, int k)` using a sliding window that tolerates at most k zeros. The demo computes Rajesh's longest success streak and the improved streak with one allowed fix.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the settlement outcomes are `1, 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1`.

Step 1: `longestOnes` starts with current zero and best zero. Day zero is a one, so current becomes one and best becomes one. Day one is a one, so current becomes two and best becomes two.

Step 2: Day two is a zero, a failure, so current resets to zero. The streak is broken and best stays two.

Step 3: Days three, four, and five are all ones, so current climbs to one, two, then three, and best updates to three at the third of them. This is the longest run.

Step 4: Day six is a zero, so current resets to zero. Days seven and eight are ones, so current climbs to one then two, but two does not beat the best three, so best stays three.

Step 5: The loop ends with best three, which is the longest streak of consecutive successful settlement days, found in one pass with only two counters.

Step 6: `longestOnesWithFlips` with k of one uses a sliding window that may include at most one zero. The window can span indices three through eight, which contains only the single zero at index six, giving a window length of six; any larger window would include two zeros and be shrunk from the left. So the improved streak with one allowed fix is six days, showing the value of bridging a single failure.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z INFO Longest success streak = 3 days
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z INFO Rajesh longest success streak: 3 days
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z INFO Longest streak allowing 1 fixes = 6 days
2026-10-26T17:40:00Z INFO With up to 1 allowed fix: 6 days
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [1,1,0,1,1,1,0,1,1]
    │
    ▼
  longestOnes (count & reset)
    │ 1,1 → current=2 best=2
    │ 0   → reset current=0
    │ 1,1,1 → current=3 best=3
    │ 0   → reset; 1,1 → current=2 (best stays 3)
    ▼ best = 3
  longestOnesWithFlips(k=1) sliding window
    │ widest window with ≤1 zero = indices 3..8 (one zero at 6)
    ▼ best = 6
  Output: streak 3; with 1 fix 6
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Max Consecutive Ones finds the longest unbroken run of ones in a binary array, and I solve it in a single pass with two counters. A current counter measures the run of ones ending at the position I am looking at, and a best counter remembers the longest run I have seen. On each one I increment the current counter and update the best; on each zero I reset the current counter to zero because the streak is broken. It is linear time and constant space.

A small but real detail is where to update the best. I update it on every one, which is always correct and avoids a special case; if you only update the best when you hit a zero, you must also update once more after the loop in case the array ends in a run of ones, which is easy to forget.

The extension I always mention is the version where you may flip at most K zeros into ones. That is a sliding window: you expand to the right and, whenever the window contains more than K zeros, you shrink from the left, tracking the widest valid window. The plain problem is just the K equals zero case, and recognising that connection shows I understand the general pattern rather than a one-off trick.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to report the longest streak of consecutive successful end-of-day settlement days for Rajesh's account as a reliability metric, and I offered the sliding-window version to answer management's what-if about the streak if the team were allowed to fix a small number of failed days. Explaining the count-and-reset logic, the update-on-every-one detail, and the sliding-window generalisation shows the interviewer that I write clean linear scans and understand how they extend to richer questions.

---

keyPoints: Fixed window: max sum of K consecutive elements
Variable window: longest substring without repeating
Expand right, shrink left based on condition
Track window state with HashMap or array
